title: Fewer of the coast-people climb to the temple
summary: In the years before the temple stands empty for good, those coast-people who still climb to Làrach an Teampaill go up fewer at a time and stay a shorter while at the top than the shepherds of the moor below ever remember them staying, a caution grown up in the climbing long before any hand carries the altar stone away.

title: A woman climbs to the temple with empty hands
summary: A shepherd of the moor watches a woman of the shore climb the temple's steps alone at first light and come down again at evening with nothing in her hands either time, and no one after her is known to climb to Làrach an Teampaill again.

title: Grass takes the temple platform
summary: With no foot left to keep it short, the grass between the temple platform's fitted stones grows up thick, and the altar's empty sockets are left to fill and empty again with nothing but whatever season sends into them.

title: Whole kin-groups come down from the abandoned heights
summary: Where ones and single families once drifted down from the empty fortress and outpost to settle at the shore, whole kin-groups now come down together, until the landing at Chwen holds more of the coast-people at once than any landing has held before.

title: The midden at Chwen outgrows the midden at Dunn
summary: The midden below the southern landing at Chwen, thickened season on season by the swelling numbers settled there, grows past the midden at Dunn, which had for a lifetime and more held the name of the largest heap of shell and bone the coast could show.

title: A landing once counted by the dozen is counted by the score
summary: A hill trader dealing at the southern shore finds a landing he had once counted by the dozen grown, within a single generation's reckoning, to a landing counted by the score, and carries the plain wonder of the count home with him.

title: The sea-way's landing-stones grooved by keels
summary: Season on season of hauled keels wear clear grooves into the flat landing-stones of the ancient sea-way along the south-east coast, so that a rower of that lane comes to know each stone by its wear as surely as by its place along the shore.

title: A father teaches his son the sea-way stone by stone
summary: A rower of the ancient sea-way carries his son in the bow through a whole season's rowing, naming each landing-stone as it comes until the boy's own eye can find the next one before his father's voice does, the same teaching the lane is given, before and after, to every rower's son.

title: Rathnait born to the valleys about the crack
summary: Rathnait is born the third child of a household two ridges east of Tobar dhìreach, of no line that keeps a fire-pot or counts fathers back to the mason by name, but of the valleys about the crack all the same.

title: An elder doubts the new name will last
summary: At the night of the lightning an old woman of the ford hears the households called Clann nan Dè for the first time and will not say the word herself, having watched other names tried at other gatherings in her own long life and none of them outlast the fire that first warmed them into being said.

title: Clann nan Dè settles into ordinary use
summary: By the time Rathnait is old enough to sit among the elders at her own hearth's turn to hold the gathering, the name Clann nan Dè is said across the valleys about the crack as plainly and as unremarked as any older name tied to a single ridge or ford.

title: Rathnait dies among the valleys she named
summary: Rathnait dies at her own household's hearth, having carried the word she first heard tried at a stranger's fire into ordinary use across the whole of the valleys about the crack.
